A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same latent-space approach to neural network verification. All 13 pages of v1.pdf and 18 pages of v3.pdf, including figures, equations, tables and appendices, are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: Tables 1–3 report original verification results and refinement, GPU/batch-size and falsification ablations, separately from results attributed to VNN-COMP.

after.justification: Tables 1–6 report original verification results and ablations, including new splitting-heuristic and approximate-versus-exact bounding comparisons in the appendices.

M1.justification: The latent-space refinement, set-based falsification and branch-and-bound framework remain. Changes concern the reported splitting procedure: v1 refines before splitting and specifies sensitive input-dimension splits; v3 splits before refinement and ranks input dimensions or unstable ReLU neurons using gradients of the output enclosure's F-radius (Section 4, Appendix B).

E1.justification: Table 1 retains all seven original benchmarks and adds linearizenn, covering neural networks for autonomous aircraft taxiing. The expanded appendix experiments otherwise use tasks already represented in the main evaluation.

E2.justification: The five main comparators—alpha-beta-CROWN, NeuralSAT, PyRAT, Marabou and nnenum—remain unchanged. Within ablations, v3 removes the center-point falsifier and separate network-wise/layer-wise refinement comparison, while adding Local Gradient and exact constrained-zonotope bounds as comparators in Tables 4 and 6.

E3.justification: Appendix A changes the evaluation hardware from an EPYC/A100 server to an i7-13700H/RTX 4070 laptop. The GPU study replaces acasxu property-specific average times and matched CPU/GPU batch sizes with acasxu/safenlp maximum times at CPU batch 1 and GPU batches 128/1024. The revised falsification study specifies 50 iterations; the new exact-bounds experiment uses 45 acasxu instances with timeouts disabled.

E4.justification: The limited refinement-count ablation becomes an eight-benchmark analysis of solved instances, subproblem counts, runtime and per-iteration overhead (Tables 2 and 5). New studies examine enclosure-gradient versus local-gradient splitting and approximate versus exact bounds (Tables 4 and 6). Conversely, network-wise versus layer-wise refinement and several matched CPU/GPU batch controls disappear.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The additional averages and maxima in v3 summarize instance workloads and computational costs rather than uncertainty across repeated runs.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes the proposed tool's solved rates from 98.9% to 99.5% on acasxu, 80.0% to 81.1% on cora, 96.0% to 97.0% on metaroom, and 84.3% to 89.2% on safenlp; linearizenn adds 100.0% (59 verified/1 falsified). These are revised results under changed settings, not isolated same-setting gains. Tables 4–6 add substantial heuristic, overhead and bounding results, including 823.3s versus 1.0s average time for exact versus approximate bounds.

T1.justification: Appendix E adds Proposition 4 and its proof, giving per-iteration complexity O(kappa q^3 + xi p q^2). Equation 13 corrects the positive/negative generator handling in v1's final interval-bound expression, Equation 10. The central unsafe-input enclosure proposition, bounding proposition and soundness corollary remain; relocating their proofs does not constitute new theory.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion shift the novelty claim from constructing a novel latent space to proposing refinement that exploits a latent space inherent in set propagation. The separate latent-space contribution is absorbed into the refinement contribution. The main claims of faster branch-and-bound verification and competitive performance remain.

C2.justification: V3 explicitly states that refinement preserves unsafe-input coverage rather than the full output enclosure. Appendix C explains why overhead can outweigh refinement benefits on low-dimensional benchmarks and how reduced batch sizes affect per-iteration costs. Appendices B and D add mechanism explanations for enclosure-gradient splitting and the practical adequacy of approximate bounds. These substantially qualify when and why acceleration occurs.

D1.justification: V3 newly discloses eight refinement iterations, at most four bounding iterations, aggregation over mutually solved instances for specified ablations, and the counterexample numerical-tolerance convention. It also updates hardware specifications. These disclosures do not establish that previously unspecified choices changed. V1's explicit main-result batch-size and automatic halving on out-of-memory errors are no longer stated.

R1.justification: V3 adds Combastel on the F-radius, Yang et al. on refinement, and Kotha et al. and Zhang et al. on neural network preimages. Section 6 adds a substantive comparison between its simultaneous constraint/dimension refinement and prior preimage approaches. Most existing related-work coverage remains.

P1.justification: The seven-section main narrative remains recognizable, with targeted rewrites of the abstract, contributions, evaluation and conclusion. Section 3 is retitled, Section 4's numbered subsections become paragraph headings, and existing implementation/proof appendices move to D/F. Acknowledgements and an LLM-use disclosure are added; much foundational prose remains unchanged.

P2.justification: V3 adopts the ICLR template, revises legends in Figures 1–3 and adds Figure 4 illustrating approximate versus exact bounds. Table 1 gains a benchmark column, the ablation displays are substantially reorganized into Tables 2–3, and Tables 4–6 add heuristic, comprehensive refinement-cost and bounding comparisons. This materially expands and restructures the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: V1's subproblem-count evidence left the practical cost of refinement and approximate bounding insufficiently tested. V3 substantially addresses these gaps through cross-benchmark runtime/overhead analyses, the exact-bounds comparison, and explicit discussion of slowdown cases, supported by complexity analysis and additional implementation details. These gains outweigh the loss of some earlier controls. Remaining weaknesses include unmatched CPU/GPU batch sizes and the incorrect claim of '60.3% more' falsifications despite Table 3b reporting 647 versus 257.
